'''Punic wax''' is '''saponified beeswax''' — beeswax boiled repeatedly with an alkali until part of it is converted to soap. The result is a wax that is partly water-soluble, spreadable cold, and has a '''melting point raised from about 60&nbsp;°C to about 100&nbsp;°C''' (140&nbsp;°F to 212&nbsp;°F). It is named for the Punics, the Carthaginians, who were a Phoenician colony.

It is also, in the Institute's reading, '''the origin point of soap technology''' — the same chemistry that makes soap, arrived at first on beeswax rather than on fat, and the material bridge between the [[Kyphi|Egyptian head cone]] material and the [[Head Cone|cone]] itself.

The operator published an '''open-source claim''' on the technique on Steemit in 2019 as ''@punicwax'': applying Punic wax to '''soap, paint and incense''', with resins, gums, rosins, oils, fats and balsams added to it — stated openly so that '''other people should copy this ancient technique made new'''. This page exists to make that claim easy to act on.

== The chemistry ==

Beeswax is not a fat but a mixture of long-chain esters, free fatty acids and hydrocarbons. The '''free acid fraction and the esters saponify''' with a strong base, producing wax soaps while the hydrocarbon fraction stays as wax. What comes out is neither wax nor soap but a hybrid: the soap fraction lets water carry it, the wax fraction gives it body and a high melting point.

=== Amphiphilic Emulsification and Transdermal Delivery ===
Because saponified beeswax contains both hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails and ionic carboxylate soap heads, it acts as a powerful amphiphilic emulsifier.
* '''Lipid-Aqueous Micro-Emulsions:''' In ancient pharmacology and cosmetics, Punic wax served as the foundational matrix for complex unguents, ointments, and medicinal pomades. It could stably bind polar botanical extracts, gums, and wines alongside non-polar plant resins ([[Kyphi]], frankincense, myrrh, pine rosin) and essential oils.
* '''Trans-Follicular Delivery:''' In [[Head Cone|Egyptian Head Cones]], Punic wax formulations allowed slow, temperature-dependent liquefaction ($37\text{–}40^\circ\text{C}$). The presence of saponified fatty acid soaps facilitated trans-follicular and transdermal penetration across the human scalp, delivering psychoactive alkaloids and aromatic terpenes directly into the cranial micro-vasculature while completely avoiding hepatic first-pass degradation.
* '''Convergence with African Saponin Systems:''' This Mediterranean saponification technology shares direct pharmacological parallels with the southern African [[Ubulawu and African Oneirogens|Ubulawu]] and [[Ukuphahla]] traditions. Where Punic wax creates amphiphilic lipid carriers through alkaline saponification of beeswax, Ubulawu utilizes high-potency plant saponins (*Helinus integrifolius*, *Silene undulata*) to generate aqueous micro-foams that lower mucosal surface tension, inhibit oral $\alpha$-amylase, and enhance sublingual permeability for ritual and ancestral dream communication.

== The traditional recipe ==

* '''150&nbsp;g''' pure beeswax
* '''Artificial seawater''': 42&nbsp;g sodium chloride in 1,200&nbsp;mL water, plus 30&nbsp;g sodium bicarbonate
* '''Boil repeatedly''' in the artificial seawater

'''Fritz Faiss''' (1905–1981) — a Bauhaus student of Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky — rediscovered the technique with Dr Hans Schmid and holds two German patents on wax preparation for encaustic. His key finding is the one to work from: '''boiling beeswax in sea water and soda three times raises the melting point from 60&nbsp;°C to 100&nbsp;°C.''' Three times. Once is not enough.

== The seven boiling procedures ==

Ordered roughly from mildest to strongest base:

# '''Salt + baking soda in water + beeswax'''
# '''Ashes + beeswax'''
# '''Ashes + salt and baking soda in water + beeswax'''
# '''Vibhuti + salt and baking soda in water + beeswax'''
# '''Sodalime + beeswax'''
# '''Potash + beeswax'''
# '''Lye + beeswax'''

Methods 1–4 are the traditional range and are what the archaeology supports. Methods 5–7 are the modern shortcut and produce a more completely saponified product.

'''Vibhuti''' — the sacred ash of Shaiva practice — is method 4's alkali, and is chemically the same class of thing as method 2's wood ash: an alkaline ash lye. That the ritual material and the working alkali are the same substance is the sort of coincidence this corpus takes seriously.

== Safety ==

* '''Stainless steel vessels only''' for methods 2–4. Corrosive bases attack many metals and etch glass.
* '''Rubber gloves.''' Keep '''vinegar''' on hand to neutralise a base splash.
* '''Avoid skin contact.''' Lye and sodalime burns are not immediately painful, which is what makes them dangerous — the damage is done before it is felt.
* Work with ventilation. Boiling alkali spits.

== The patent literature ==

Three documented routes beyond the traditional one:

* '''Kreidezeit method''' — bleached wax saponified with '''potash'''; the result is partly water-soluble and easy to apply.
* '''French patent FR2559778A1 — the desert-grass method.''' Uses '''yellow wax dust (cuticle dust) from desert and steppe grass''' rather than beeswax. Boil in saturated brine with sodium hydroxide powder → cool the white pasty wax in cold water → purify by boiling in water containing iron oxide → cool in pure water → sun bleach → reactive cooking with a metal catalyst → separate catalyst by boiling in water → final sun bleaching. Yields a white wax with a high melting temperature.
* '''German patent DE202006013438U1 — "Punic milk."''' Beeswax, potash (K₂CO₃), water and '''sodium water-glass (Na₂SiO₃)'''. Uses given: coating, adhesive, impregnating agent, building material, restoration material.

== The archaeology that vindicated it ==

'''Cuní, Cuni, Eisen, Savizky and Bové (2012)''' analysed eight Roman wall paintings from Spain and a Roman-Egyptian mummy portrait by '''ATR-FTIR and GC-MS''', and found the binding medium was '''beeswax and soap'''. Their conclusion: this is the first demonstration that the Romans used a '''water-soluble wax-and-soap encaustic paint''', and that wax-and-soap may be the lost ancient encaustic formulation that has been searched for for five hundred years.

That is the point at which Punic wax stops being a craft revival and becomes a solved archaeological problem.

== Encaustic ==

'''Encaustic''' is painting with heated wax as the binding medium — the technique of the Fayum mummy portraits, whose colours have survived two thousand years. Ordinary beeswax encaustic must be kept molten. '''Punic wax, being partly water-soluble, can be worked cold and thinned with water''', which is what makes it practical rather than merely historical.

== The Punic Wax Network, and why the Beauty Economy is named for the same reaction ==

'''Punic wax is the origin point of soap technology''' — saponification arrived at first on beeswax rather than on fat — and the ecosystem now called the [[Van Kush Family]] was originally named for it.

'''The name came before the brand.''' Posting on Bitcointalk as '''Tokenista''' on '''6 April 2021''', five months before [[VKBT and CURE|VKBT]] existed and before "Van Kush Family" was an institution:

''"'''The Punic Wax Network is what I am creating.''' It is going to be Mining Pools, Witnesses, as well as Mining for our own Clone of each and every type of Blockchain and Token. Then we will teach others also, and all of this will be on PunicWax.com."''

And two days later, on '''8 April 2021''':

''"That is why I am starting the Punic Wax network, to teach other people to do it for them themselves and others, with a kind of Help Desk community different from those provide by the Bitcoin Foundation."''

The chain handle '''@punicwax''' is the one the ''Van Kush Family Guide to the Game'' was published under — the guide whose title, misread across a line break, gave the Family its name. The earlier tokens were named the same way: '''Punic Copper''' and '''Punic Tin''', announced on Bitcointalk on '''14 November 2020''' as ''"The 1st Punic Currency in 2,000 Years"'', and meant for trading the materials of a religious life. The founder's rule for them, quoted in the 2026 chain post ''Belief, Attention and Intent'': ''"You must Ground your Currency, like with Electric Current, by Exchanging it for Plants, Metals and Gemstones."''

'''The reaction is the link, and it is not a metaphor.''' The '''Van Kush Beauty Economy''' — announced on Blurt on 1 November 2021 — is an economy of soap, wax, cosmetics and herbs, which is to say an economy of '''saponified goods'''. Punic wax is the oldest documented instance of that same alkaline hydrolysis, performed on wax instead of tallow, and it is the technique the operator published an open-source claim on under the @punicwax name in 2019 precisely so that others would copy it. '''The network was named for the chemistry of the goods''', and the goods and the network are the same claim made twice: that an old, specific, repeatable procedure is worth more in public than held back.

In the same 2026 post the wax is treated as a carrier of transmission generally — the Egyptian Magic cream recipe passed across a diner table in 1986, the [[Head Cone|head cones]] confirmed as real objects at Amarna, [[Kyphi]] carved on the walls at Philae and Edfu, and Punic wax found again and shared on the chains for years.

== Carthaginian context ==

The Punics were the people of Carthage, originally a Phoenician colony in what is now Tunisia and Libya. The Institute's reading connects this to the Tyre line: '''2 Samuel 5:11''' records Hiram king of Tyre sending cedar and stonemasons to David, and the same Tyre founded Carthage. Blavatsky's line is quoted in the source material — ''"Not only were Moors well versed in it, they were the originators of [Mystery Schools]."'' That framing is the Institute's, not established history.

'''And Carthage lost.''' Any argument that leans on Carthage has to concede the outcome first: Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE, and the claim a Punic framing makes is about '''position''' — the older equipment, the farming colonies, the libraries, the wax — not about who won.

Two corrections worth carrying, because this library's own interest is in the places where popular accounts have lost their citations:

* '''Rome did not sow Carthage with salt.''' '''No ancient source says so.''' R. T. Ridley set the problem out in ''"To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt: The Destruction of Carthage"'', ''Classical Philology'' 81 (1986), 140–146, and found the earliest reference he could locate to be modern; the detail appears to have been conflated with the genuine salting of Shechem at Judges 9:45. The earliest printed appearance so far identified is '''1858''', in the ''New American Cyclopaedia''; its persistence is usually traced to B. L. Hallward's chapter in the ''Cambridge Ancient History'' vol. 8 (1930), which states it without a reference. Ancient writers describe the city reduced to dust or ploughed over — never salted.
* '''The real loss was a book, and it is better evidence.''' Pliny (''Natural History'' 18.22–23), Varro (''Res Rusticae'' 1.1.10) and Columella (1.1.13) record that '''Mago's''' agricultural treatise ran to '''28 volumes''', that the Roman Senate had it '''translated by decree''' — Pliny's ''unius eius'', that one man's work alone — while the other Carthaginian libraries were given away rather than burned; and that '''all three later versions are themselves now lost'''. A conqueror who translates one book by senatorial decree and then loses the translation is a sharper story than a field of salt that nobody sowed.

== Coverage ==
Covers the chemistry of saponified beeswax, the traditional recipe and the seven boiling procedures with their safety requirements, the patent literature, the 2012 analysis that turned the technique from a craft revival into a solved archaeological problem, and encaustic. '''Adds the Punic Wax Network''' — the ecosystem's original name, dated to April 2021 from the founder's own Bitcointalk posts, five months before VKBT — the Punic Copper and Punic Tin tokens of November 2020, and the reason the Beauty Economy carries the name of the same reaction: both are economies of saponified goods, and both were published open so that others would copy them. The Carthaginian framing is kept as the Institute's reading and marked as such, with Carthage's defeat conceded before the frame is used, the salting of Carthage identified as a modern myth with its printing history, and Mago's translated-then-lost treatise given as the better-sourced loss. Not covered: commercial supply of any of these materials, and the Blavatsky Mystery-School claim beyond noting it is the Institute's framing rather than established history.
